name: Vitamin A palmitate lip

card.summary: Vitamin A palmitate (retinyl palmitate) in lip products is used as a conditioning ingredient to keep lips smoother and healthier-looking.
card.note: Vitamin A in topical products is generally avoided in pregnancy unless a clinician advises otherwise.

quick.overview:
Retinyl palmitate is vitamin A bound to palmitic acid and is a common form of vitamin A in topical skincare products. In lip care it is added to balms and treatments for conditioning.

The payoff people are after is smoother, less chapped lips with a better surface for lip color or a naturally even look.
quick.how: It is applied in a lip balm or treatment as part of a regular lip routine. The occlusive base of a balm (wax or petrolatum) seals in moisture, with the vitamin as an added ingredient.
quick.risks: Absorbed retinyl palmitate is converted to retinol and then retinoic acid, though not efficiently. Animal studies on retinyl palmitate in sunlight raised questions that remain discussed in toxicology reviews. Pregnant people typically ask a clinician about vitamin A products.

lead: Vitamin A palmitate, or retinyl palmitate, is an ester of retinol and palmitic acid and the main form in which animals store vitamin A. It is used as a supplement, a milk fortifier, and an ingredient in some topical skin products [1].

Lip balms work mainly by forming an occlusive layer that holds in moisture and shields lips from wind and dry air; added ingredients such as sunscreens or medicaments can add specific benefits [2]. Vitamin A palmitate is one such addition in some products.
No clinical trial of retinyl palmitate specifically for lips has been located.

chain: Balm base holds moisture on the lips
Retinyl palmitate included as a conditioning ingredient
angle.text: People use vitamin A-containing balms to keep lips soft and smooth-looking. The balm base itself does the moisture-sealing.

infobox: Converted to retinol, then retinoic acid, inefficiently in skin

paras: After absorption through skin, retinyl palmitate is converted to retinol and then to retinoic acid, the active form of vitamin A, though neither absorption nor conversion is very efficient [1].

High topical doses in laboratory animals were linked to accelerated cancer, raising sunscreen concerns; one toxicological review found no convincing evidence that retinyl palmitate in sunscreens is carcinogenic, while a later National Toxicology Program study reported more tumors in sunlight-exposed mice given retinoic acid or retinyl palmitate [1]. The WHO notes preformed vitamin A intake should not exceed the recommended allowance in pregnancy, since overdose can cause hypervitaminosis A [1].
No studies found of retinyl palmitate in lip products.
